glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Bezalel completes the bronze altar, the bronze laver, and the courtyard with its gate, and the chapter closes with a careful account of the gold, silver, and bronze given for the work, including the ransom silver that became the foundation of the sanctuary.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Exodus 38 continues the building of the tabernacle (chapters 35–40), following the instructions of 27:1–19 and 30:17–21. The furnishings of the tent were finished in chapter 37.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, made all that the LORD had commanded Moses.” (Exodus 38:22)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
The work moves out into the courtyard. Bezalel makes the great bronze altar of burnt offering, square and hollow, with horns at its corners and bronze tools for the sacrifices. Beside it he makes the bronze laver, the basin where the priests would wash, “from the bronze mirrors of the serving women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting” (38:8). Women who served at the entrance gave up their mirrors so that priests could be cleansed. Around everything rise the white linen hangings of the court, with one wide, beautiful gate on the east side.

Then the chapter does something unexpected: it counts. At Moses’ command, under the oversight of Aaron’s son Ithamar, the materials are recorded. Bezalel “made all that the LORD had commanded Moses” (38:22), with Aholiab beside him. The gold is weighed, then the silver. The silver came from the half shekel paid by every man counted in the census, 603,550 men, rich and poor alike giving the same ransom (30:15). That silver was cast into the sockets of the sanctuary and of the veil, and the rest was used for the hooks, tops, and bands of the pillars (38:27–28). Those sockets supported the frames of the dwelling, so the house of God stood on silver given as a ransom, a picture of redemption.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Exodus 38:1–8 — The Bronze Altar and the Laver

Bezalel makes the square altar of burnt offering of acacia wood covered with bronze, with its horns, tools, grate, rings, and poles. He makes the bronze laver and its stand from the bronze mirrors of the women who served at the entrance of the tabernacle.

Exodus 38:9–20 — The Courtyard and Its Gate

The courtyard is enclosed with linen hangings on pillars with bronze sockets and silver hooks and bands, one hundred cubits on the long sides and fifty on the ends. A woven screen twenty cubits wide forms the gate, and all the pegs are bronze.

Exodus 38:21–23 — The Inventory Under Ithamar and the Work of Bezalel and Aholiab

At Moses’ command the materials of the tabernacle are recorded for the Levites’ service under the oversight of Ithamar, Aaron’s son. Bezalel made everything the LORD commanded Moses, with Aholiab as engraver, designer, and weaver.

Exodus 38:24–31 — The Gold, Silver, and Bronze Used in the Work

The gold used for the holy place, the silver from the half shekel paid by each of the 603,550 men counted, and the bronze offering are all recorded. The silver becomes the sockets of the sanctuary and the veil and the hooks and bands of the pillars, while the bronze makes the door sockets, the altar, the court sockets, and the pegs.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Exodus 38 shows that gifts given to God’s work deserve careful accounting. Moses ordered an inventory, and every talent of gold, silver, and bronze was recorded. Paul followed the same principle when he handled the churches’ gifts with care so that no one could fault the ministry (2 Corinthians 8:20–21).

The chapter also gives a striking picture of redemption. The silver from the equal ransom paid by every counted man furnished the sockets beneath the sanctuary and the veil. That fact pictures God’s dwelling among His people resting on their redemption. The bronze altar and the laver point to Jesus, who gave Himself once for all and who cleanses His people so that they can serve Him (Hebrews 10:10–14; Ephesians 5:25–27).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Sacrifice and cleansing in the court. The bronze altar and the laver stand in the courtyard (38:1–8).

Gifts from serving women. The laver is made from mirrors given by women who served at the tent’s entrance (38:8).

Obedience to the pattern. Bezalel makes all that the LORD commanded Moses (38:22).

Accountability for offerings. The materials are counted and recorded at Moses’ command (38:21, 24–31).

Built on redemption. The ransom silver becomes the sockets of the sanctuary and veil (38:25–27).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Laver (38:8). The bronze basin for the priests’ washing, made from donated bronze mirrors.

Ithamar (38:21). Aaron’s youngest son, who oversaw the inventory of the tabernacle.

Bekah (38:26). Half a shekel, the ransom each counted man paid (30:13–15).

603,550 men (38:26). The number of men twenty years and older counted in the census, as written (compare Numbers 1:46).

Sockets (38:27). Silver bases that held up the boards of the sanctuary and the pillars of the veil.

focus: Exodus 38 completes the furnishings of the courtyard, the bronze altar and the bronze laver, and the courtyard itself with its hangings and gate. The chapter then gives an inventory of the gold, silver, and bronze used for the work, noting that the silver came from the ransom paid by every man counted in the census.

sections.title: The Bronze Altar and the Laver
sections.summary: Bezalel makes the square altar of burnt offering of acacia wood overlaid with bronze, with its horns, utensils, grate, rings, and poles. He makes the bronze laver and its base “from the bronze mirrors of the serving women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting” (Exodus 38:8).

sections.title: The Courtyard and Its Gate
sections.summary: The courtyard is enclosed with hangings of fine linen on pillars with bronze sockets and silver hooks and bands, one hundred cubits on the south and north and fifty on the west and east. A woven screen twenty cubits long forms the gate of the court, and all the pegs are bronze.

sections.title: The Inventory Under Ithamar and the Work of Bezalel and Aholiab
sections.summary: At Moses’ command the inventory of the tabernacle of the Testimony is counted for the service of the Levites under the oversight of Ithamar, son of Aaron the priest. The work itself was made by Bezalel, who “made all that the LORD had commanded Moses” (Exodus 38:22), with Aholiab the engraver, designer, and weaver.

sections.title: The Gold, Silver, and Bronze Used in the Work
sections.summary: The gold of the offering used in the holy place totals twenty-nine talents and 730 shekels, and the silver, a half shekel from each of 603,550 men counted, totals one hundred talents and 1,775 shekels, cast into the sockets of the sanctuary and the veil and into hooks and bands. The bronze offering of seventy talents and 2,400 shekels makes the sockets for the door, the bronze altar and its utensils, the court sockets, and the pegs.

1.brief: Bezalel makes the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood, five cubits square and three cubits high. The great altar of the courtyard is made.
1.explain:
“He made the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood;”

Bezalel makes “the altar of burnt offering” for the courtyard (27:1–8).

“five cubits was its length and five cubits its width—it was square—and its height was three cubits.”

The altar is square, five cubits on each side, about 7½ feet, and three cubits high, about 4½ feet, just as the pattern required (27:1).

2.brief: Bezalel makes its horns on the four corners, of one piece with it, and overlays it with bronze. The altar follows God’s pattern.
2.explain:
“He made its horns on its four corners; the horns were of one piece with it. And he overlaid it with bronze.”

The horns rise from the four corners and are of one piece with the altar, not attached afterward (27:2). Blood from the sin offerings was later put on these horns (29:12; Leviticus 4:25). The bronze overlay protected the wood from the fire.

3.brief: Bezalel makes all the altar’s utensils of bronze: pans, shovels, basins, forks, and firepans. The tools for sacrifice are provided.
3.explain:
“He made all the utensils for the altar: the pans, the shovels, the basins, the forks, and the firepans; all its utensils he made of bronze.”

Each utensil served the work of sacrifice: pans to receive the ashes, shovels for gathering them, basins, probably for the blood of the sacrifices, forks for handling the meat, and firepans for carrying coals (27:3).

4.brief: Bezalel makes a bronze grate under the rim, halfway up. The grate is set within the altar.
4.explain:
“And he made a grate of bronze network for the altar, under its rim, midway from the bottom.”

The bronze grate is set midway up the altar (27:4–5).

5.brief: Bezalel casts four rings for the corners of the grate as holders for the poles. The altar is prepared for carrying.
5.explain:
“He cast four rings for the four corners of the bronze grating, as holders for the poles.”

The rings hold the poles.

6.brief: Bezalel makes the poles of acacia wood and overlays them with bronze. The carrying poles are finished.
6.explain:
“And he made the poles of acacia wood, and overlaid them with bronze.”

The carrying poles are finished (27:6).

7.brief: Bezalel puts the poles through the rings on the sides of the altar and makes it hollow with boards. The altar is completed as God showed Moses.
7.explain:
“Then he put the poles into the rings on the sides of the altar, with which to bear it.”

The altar is ready to travel.

“He made the altar hollow with boards.”

It is “hollow,” as God showed Moses (27:8). The bronze altar points to Christ’s once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:10–14).

8.brief: Bezalel makes the bronze laver and its base “from the bronze mirrors of the serving women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting.” The women’s gift and service become part of the sanctuary.
8.explain:
“He made the laver of bronze and its base of bronze,”

The “laver” for the priests’ washing is made (30:17–21).

“from the bronze mirrors of the serving women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting.”

The bronze came from “the bronze mirrors” of women who served “at the door of the tabernacle of meeting.” Mirrors of polished bronze were valued possessions. These women gave them for God’s house. The text records their service and their gift but gives the mirrors no further meaning. The laver’s purpose is washing, a picture of the cleansing Christ gives (Ephesians 5:25–27).
8.notes: 1 Samuel 2:22 also mentions women who served at the door of the tabernacle of meeting. The text does not explain what their service involved.

9.brief: Bezalel makes the court with hangings of fine linen one hundred cubits long on the south side. The courtyard is built.
9.explain:
“Then he made the court on the south side; the hangings of the court were of fine woven linen, one hundred cubits long.”

The court is a fenced enclosure around the tabernacle. Its south side is a wall of fine linen hangings one hundred cubits long, about 150 feet (27:9).

10.brief: The south side has twenty pillars with bronze sockets, and silver hooks and bands. The court’s structure matches the pattern.
10.explain:
“There were twenty pillars for them, with twenty bronze sockets. The hooks of the pillars and their bands were silver.”

Twenty pillars set in bronze sockets hold up the south hangings. Silver hooks and bands at the top of each pillar hold the linen in place (27:10).

11.brief: The north side has one hundred cubits of hangings, twenty pillars with bronze sockets, and silver hooks and bands. The long sides match.
11.explain:
“On the north side the hangings were one hundred cubits long, with twenty pillars and their twenty bronze sockets.”

The north side matches the south: another hundred cubits of hangings on twenty pillars in bronze sockets (27:11). The two long sides run parallel.

“The hooks of the pillars and their bands were silver.”

The same silver hooks and bands crown the pillars of the north side, so silver fittings top every pillar of both long walls.

12.brief: The west side has fifty cubits of hangings with ten pillars and sockets and silver hooks and bands. The back of the court is closed.
12.explain:
“And on the west side there were hangings of fifty cubits, with ten pillars and their ten sockets. The hooks of the pillars and their bands were silver.”

The west side, at the back, is shorter: fifty cubits of hangings on ten pillars, with the same silver fittings (27:12). With the two long sides it encloses the court on three sides, and the east side holds the gate (38:13–15).

13.brief: The east side is fifty cubits wide. The front of the court faces east.
13.explain:
“For the east side the hangings were fifty cubits.”

The front faces east (27:13).

14.brief: The hangings on one side of the gate are fifteen cubits with three pillars and sockets. The entrance is framed.
14.explain:
“The hangings of one side of the gate were fifteen cubits long, with their three pillars and their three sockets,”

The entrance is framed on one side (27:14).

15.brief: The other side of the gate also has fifteen cubits of hangings with three pillars and sockets. The gate is framed on both sides.
15.explain:
“and the same for the other side of the court gate; on this side and that were hangings of fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and their three sockets.”

The gate is framed on both sides (27:15).

16.brief: All the hangings around the court are of fine woven linen. The court’s walls are uniform.
16.explain:
“All the hangings of the court all around were of fine woven linen.”

The court’s walls are uniform white linen.

17.brief: The pillars’ sockets are bronze, their hooks and bands silver, and their capitals overlaid with silver. The court is finished with care.
17.explain:
“The sockets for the pillars were bronze, the hooks of the pillars and their bands were silver,”

The pillars stand on bronze with silver fittings (27:17).

“and the overlay of their capitals was silver; and all the pillars of the court had bands of silver.”

The tops of the pillars are overlaid with silver. The court is finished with care.

18.brief: The screen for the court gate is woven of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, twenty cubits long and five high. The one entrance into the court is beautiful and wide.
18.explain:
“The screen for the gate of the court was woven of blue, purple, and scarlet thread, and of fine woven linen.”

The gate’s screen is colorful, standing out from the white walls (27:16).

“The length was twenty cubits, and the height along its width was five cubits, corresponding to the hangings of the court.”

The one entrance into the court is beautiful and wide. It pictures Jesus, the way to the Father (John 14:6).

19.brief: The gate has four pillars with bronze sockets, silver hooks, and silver-overlaid capitals and bands. The gate is completed.
19.explain:
“And there were four pillars with their four sockets of bronze; their hooks were silver, and the overlay of their capitals and their bands was silver.”

The gate’s pillars are completed.

20.brief: All the pegs of the tabernacle and the court are bronze. Even the smallest parts are finished.
20.explain:
“All the pegs of the tabernacle, and of the court all around, were bronze.”

Even the smallest parts are finished (27:19).

21.brief: The inventory of the tabernacle of the Testimony is counted at Moses’ command for the service of the Levites under the oversight of Ithamar, son of Aaron the priest. The record is kept carefully and with accountability.
21.explain:
“This is the inventory of the tabernacle, the tabernacle of the Testimony,”

The chapter turns to an “inventory,” an accounting of the materials used.

“which was counted according to the commandment of Moses, for the service of the Levites, by the hand of Ithamar, son of Aaron the priest.”

The count was made at Moses’ command under the oversight of “Ithamar,” Aaron’s son. The gifts entrusted to God’s work were carefully accounted for.

22.brief: Bezalel of the tribe of Judah “made all that the LORD had commanded Moses.” The chief craftsman’s work is credited as full obedience to God’s word.
22.explain:
“Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, made all that the LORD had commanded Moses.”

Bezalel “made all that the LORD had commanded.” His work is credited as full obedience to God’s word.

23.brief: With Bezalel is Aholiab of the tribe of Dan, an engraver, designer, and weaver in colored thread and fine linen. Aholiab is honored for his part in the work.
23.explain:
“And with him was Aholiab the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, an engraver and designer, a weaver of blue, purple, and scarlet thread, and of fine linen.”

“Aholiab” is honored as engraver, designer, and weaver. Both named workers have their place.

24.brief: The gold used in all the work of the holy place is twenty-nine talents and 730 shekels by the sanctuary shekel. The record shows how much gold the people gave.
24.explain:
“All the gold that was used in all the work of the holy place, that is, the gold of the offering,”

The gold came from the people’s offering (35:22).

“was twenty-nine talents and seven hundred and thirty shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary.”

This is the total of the gold freely offered by the people (35:22). Moses records the amount so that the use of the offering is accounted for (38:21).
24.notes: Modern equivalents are estimates, since the exact weight of a talent and shekel is uncertain. By common estimates the gold weighed roughly a ton.

25.brief: The silver from those counted in the congregation is one hundred talents and 1,775 shekels. The silver came from the ransom paid at the census.
25.explain:
“And the silver from those who were numbered of the congregation”

The silver came “from those who were numbered,” the ransom paid at the census (30:11–16).

“was one hundred talents and one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary:”

The silver came to one hundred talents and 1,775 shekels. The next three verses show how that total was reached and how every part of it was used.

26.brief: A bekah, half a shekel, was given by each man twenty years old and above, 603,550 men in all. Every counted man gave the same amount, as Exodus 30:15 required.
26.explain:
“a bekah for each man (that is, half a shekel, according to the shekel of the sanctuary),”

Each man gave “a bekah,” half a shekel, as 30:13–15 required.

“for everyone included in the numbering from twenty years old and above, for six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty men.”

The same number appears in the census of Numbers 1:46. At half a shekel each, 603,550 men gave 301,775 shekels. Since a talent equals 3,000 shekels, that is exactly one hundred talents and 1,775 shekels, the total in 38:25. Every counted man gave the same amount.

27.brief: The hundred talents of silver are cast into the hundred sockets of the sanctuary and the veil, one talent per socket. The ransom silver becomes the foundation of the sanctuary.
27.explain:
“And from the hundred talents of silver were cast the sockets of the sanctuary and the bases of the veil:”

The ransom silver became “the sockets of the sanctuary” and the bases of the veil’s pillars.

“one hundred sockets from the hundred talents, one talent for each socket.”

Each socket used a talent of silver. The tabernacle literally stood on the ransom paid for the people’s lives. The people among whom God dwelt stood on His redeeming provision.
27.notes: The hundred sockets were the ninety-six under the boards (26:19–25) and the four under the veil’s pillars (26:32).

28.brief: From the 1,775 shekels Bezalel makes hooks for the pillars and overlays their capitals and makes their bands. Every portion of the silver is used.
28.explain:
“Then from the one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five shekels he made hooks for the pillars, overlaid their capitals, and made bands for them.”

The remaining silver became hooks, caps, and bands. Every portion of the silver was used.

29.brief: The bronze offering is seventy talents and 2,400 shekels. The bronze given is recorded.
29.explain:
“The offering of bronze was seventy talents and two thousand four hundred shekels.”

Bronze came to seventy talents and 2,400 shekels. The next two verses record how it was used: the sockets for the door of the tabernacle, the bronze altar with its grating and utensils, the sockets of the court and its gate, and the pegs (38:30–31).

30.brief: With the bronze Bezalel makes the sockets for the door of the tabernacle, the bronze altar, its grate, and all its utensils. The bronze serves the entrance and the altar.
30.explain:
“And with it he made the sockets for the door of the tabernacle of meeting, the bronze altar, the bronze grating for it, and all the utensils for the altar,”

The bronze served the entrance and the altar.

31.brief: The bronze also makes the sockets of the court and its gate and all the pegs for the tabernacle and court. The inventory accounts carefully for how the bronze was used.
31.explain:
“the sockets for the court all around, the bases for the court gate, all the pegs for the tabernacle, and all the pegs for the court all around.”

It also made the court’s sockets and pegs. The inventory accounts carefully for how the bronze was used.
